implementation_notes: C# has two channel-like primitives and the choice matters. System.Threading.Channels.Channel<T> is the general answer: a bounded or unbounded async channel with WriteAsync/ReadAsync, Complete() (the producer's close), and a built-in multi-reader/multi-writer design - use it for a work queue or a producer-consumer pipeline. For a synchronous bounded channel, BlockingCollection<T> is the right choice (bounded capacity, GetConsumingEnumerable, CompleteAdding) and it composes with Parallel.ForEach. For a thread-pool work queue, a ConcurrentQueue plus a semaphore signalling item availability is the standard construction (and ConcurrentQueue is itself a lock-free ring). The channel's close maps to Complete()/CompleteAdding(): after completion, ReadAsync drains the remaining items and then returns false/channel-closed, which is exactly the Go semantics.
idiom_name: System.Threading.Channels.Channel<T> (async, bounded/unbounded, Complete() closes) or BlockingCollection<T> (synchronous, bounded)
pitfalls: You must call Complete()/CompleteAdding() or every reader blocks forever after the producer exits - the classic hang.
BoundedChannelFullMode: Wait (backpressure) vs DropWrite vs DropOldest - the last two silently drop, so choose deliberately for a 'latest value' stream only.
BlockingCollection.GetConsumingEnumerable() must be consumed exactly once; a second enumeration is undefined and can lose items.
ReadAsync on a completed-and-drained channel returns false (ChannelClosedException in some paths) - handle termination, do not treat it as 'try again'.
Cancellation on ReadAsync/WriteAsync must be honoured and the item may be lost on a cancelled write; use onUndelivered-style handling if the resource must be released.
